Study order and the two common traps

HW5 23.5 → 23.7 → textbook 22.40 → 22.42 → Tutorial 7 Q1–2 → Tutorial 6 Q47/Q69 → textbook 24.34–36 → 22.50 → HW7 24.66/24.68.

At closest approach two freely moving particles share a velocity; both are at rest only in the centre-of-mass frame. A connected battery fixes the network voltage, not every internal capacitor voltage.

12μ(v1i−v2i)2+kq1q2ri=kq1q2rmin⁡,μ=m1m2m1+m2.\frac12\mu(v_{1i}-v_{2i})^2+\frac{kq_1q_2}{r_i}=\frac{kq_1q_2}{r_{\min}},\quad\mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}.21​μ(v1i​−v2i​)2+ri​kq1​q2​​=rmin​kq1​q2​​,μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​.

This head-on, nonrelativistic closest-approach equation assumes repelling charges and no external work. For a fixed target, use the moving particle’s mass instead of the two-body reduced mass.

Homework 4 · 22.15Excess electrons on a conducting sphereSupporting · Gauss & conductors
Original question screenshot

Cropped to question 22.15, with its diagrams and any continuation included. Click an image to enlarge.

A spherical conductor has diameter 26.0 cm. How many excess electrons produce a field magnitude of 1150 N/C just outside its surface?

Original problem set ↗Existing homework practice ↗Link to question
Show worked solution

Tesselate explanation

  1. Identify

    An isolated spherical conductor has its excess charge on the surface. Added electrons make Q negative, so the external field points inward.

  2. Set up

    For a concentric Gaussian sphere just outside the metal, ∣Q∣=ε0E(4πR2)|Q|=\varepsilon_0 E(4\pi R^2)∣Q∣=ε0​E(4πR2) and N=∣Q∣/eN=|Q|/eN=∣Q∣/e.

  3. Execute

    R=0.260/2=0.130 mR=0.260/2=0.130\ \mathrm mR=0.260/2=0.130 m ∣Q∣=4π(8.854×10−12)(1150)(0.130)2=2.16×10−9 C|Q|=4\pi(8.854\times10^{-12})(1150)(0.130)^2=2.16\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm C∣Q∣=4π(8.854×10−12)(1150)(0.130)2=2.16×10−9 C N=2.16×10−91.602×10−19=1.35×1010N=\frac{2.16\times10^{-9}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}=1.35\times10^{10}N=1.602×10−192.16×10−9​=1.35×1010

  4. Evaluate

    The count is positive, while Q = −2.16 nC. Using the diameter as R would give four times too many electrons. Manual problem 22.15 uses a different question.

1.35 × 10¹⁰ excess electrons; Q = −2.16 nC.

Homework 4 · 22.19Charge inside a conducting shellCore · Gauss & conductors
Original question screenshot

Cropped to question 22.19, with its diagrams and any continuation included. Click an image to enlarge.

A conducting spherical shell has outer radius 0.250 m, inner radius 0.200 m, and initial surface charge density +6.37 × 10⁻⁶ C/m². Place −0.500 µC at the centre of its cavity. Find (a) the new outer surface density, (b) the field just outside, and (c) the flux through a sphere just inside the cavity wall.

Original problem set ↗Existing homework practice ↗Link to question
Show worked solution

Tesselate explanation

  1. Identify

    Initially the empty cavity has no inner surface charge. The shell is isolated, so introducing the central charge redistributes its charge without changing its total.

  2. Set up

    Qs=4πb2σ0,Qi=−q,Qo=Qs−Qi=Qs+qQ_s=4\pi b^2\sigma_0,\quad Q_i=-q,\quad Q_o=Q_s-Q_i=Q_s+qQs​=4πb2σ0​,Qi​=−q,Qo​=Qs​−Qi​=Qs​+q σo=Qo4πb2,E(b+)=Qo4πε0b2,Φ(a−)=qε0\sigma_o=\frac{Q_o}{4\pi b^2},\quad E(b^+)=\frac{Q_o}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 b^2},\quad \Phi(a^-)=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}σo​=4πb2Qo​​,E(b+)=4πε0​b2Qo​​,Φ(a−)=ε0​q​

  3. Execute

    Qs=5.003 μC,Qi=+0.500 μC,Qo=4.503 μCQ_s=5.003\ \mu\mathrm C,\quad Q_i=+0.500\ \mu\mathrm C,\quad Q_o=4.503\ \mu\mathrm CQs​=5.003 μC,Qi​=+0.500 μC,Qo​=4.503 μC (a) σo=+5.73×10−6 C/m2(a)\ \sigma_o=+5.73\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C/m^2}(a) σo​=+5.73×10−6 C/m2 (b) E=6.48×105 N/C radially outward(b)\ E=6.48\times10^5\ \mathrm{N/C}\ \text{radially outward}(b) E=6.48×105 N/C radially outward (c) Φ=−5.65×104 N m2/C(c)\ \Phi=-5.65\times10^4\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C}(c) Φ=−5.65×104 Nm2/C

  4. Evaluate

    The shell still totals +5.003 µC. The cavity Gaussian sphere encloses only the negative point charge, so its outward flux is negative. The manual rounds intermediate values and gives 6.47 × 10⁵ N/C; both agree within rounding.

(a) +5.73 × 10⁻⁶ C/m²; (b) 6.48 × 10⁵ N/C outward; (c) −5.65 × 10⁴ N m²/C.

Homework 4 · 22.21Uniformly charged insulating sphereCore · Bonus · spherical charge
Original question screenshot

Cropped to question 22.21, with its diagrams and any continuation included. Click an image to enlarge.

A solid insulating sphere has radius 0.355 m. The field magnitude 0.145 m beyond its surface is 1750 N/C. Find (a) its uniform volume charge density and (b) the field magnitude 0.200 m from its centre.

Original problem set ↗Existing homework practice ↗Link to question
Show worked solution

Tesselate explanation

  1. Identify

    Use spherical symmetry. Outside the sphere all its charge is enclosed. Inside a uniformly charged insulator, enclosed charge grows as r³; the electric field need not be zero.

  2. Set up

    Q=4πε0Eoutrout2,∣ρ∣=∣Q∣(4/3)πR3Q=4\pi\varepsilon_0 E_{out}r_{out}^2,\quad |\rho|=\frac{|Q|}{(4/3)\pi R^3}Q=4πε0​Eout​rout2​,∣ρ∣=(4/3)πR3∣Q∣​ Qenc=ρ4πr33,∣E(r)∣=∣ρ∣r3ε0Q_{enc}=\rho\frac{4\pi r^3}{3},\quad |E(r)|=\frac{|\rho|r}{3\varepsilon_0}Qenc​=ρ34πr3​,∣E(r)∣=3ε0​∣ρ∣r​

  3. Execute

    rout=0.355+0.145=0.500 m,∣Q∣=4.87×10−8 Cr_{out}=0.355+0.145=0.500\ \mathrm m,\quad |Q|=4.87\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm Crout​=0.355+0.145=0.500 m,∣Q∣=4.87×10−8 C (a) ∣ρ∣=2.60×10−7 C/m3(a)\ |\rho|=2.60\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{C/m^3}(a) ∣ρ∣=2.60×10−7 C/m3 (b) ∣E(0.200)∣=1.96×103 N/C(b)\ |E(0.200)|=1.96\times10^3\ \mathrm{N/C}(b) ∣E(0.200)∣=1.96×103 N/C

  4. Evaluate

    Only a field magnitude is specified, so the sign of the charge is not determined. For positive charge the field is outward; for negative charge it is inward. Inside, E grows linearly from zero at the centre, then falls as 1/r² outside.

|ρ| = 2.60 × 10⁻⁷ C/m³; |E(0.200 m)| = 1.96 × 10³ N/C.

Original question screenshot

Cropped to question 22.33, with its diagrams and any continuation included. Click an image to enlarge.

A sphere of mass 4.00 × 10⁻⁶ kg and charge +5.00 × 10⁻⁸ C hangs beside a very large insulating sheet with surface charge density −2.50 × 10⁻⁹ C/m². Find the thread angle from vertical.

Original problem set ↗Existing homework practice ↗Link to question
Show worked solution

Tesselate explanation

  1. Identify

    The positive sphere is attracted toward the negative sheet. Three forces balance: tension along the thread, weight downward, and electric force toward the sheet.

  2. Set up

    For a very large insulating sheet, E=∣σ∣/(2ε0)E=|\sigma|/(2\varepsilon_0)E=∣σ∣/(2ε0​). Tsin⁡θ=qE,Tcos⁡θ=mg,tan⁡θ=q∣σ∣2ε0mgT\sin\theta=qE,\quad T\cos\theta=mg,\quad \tan\theta=\frac{q|\sigma|}{2\varepsilon_0 mg}Tsinθ=qE,Tcosθ=mg,tanθ=2ε0​mgq∣σ∣​

  3. Execute

    E=141.2 N/C,Fe=7.06×10−6 N,mg=3.92×10−5 NE=141.2\ \mathrm{N/C},\quad F_e=7.06\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm N,\quad mg=3.92\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm NE=141.2 N/C,Fe​=7.06×10−6 N,mg=3.92×10−5 N θ=tan⁡−1(0.1801)=10.2∘\theta=\tan^{-1}(0.1801)=10.2^\circθ=tan−1(0.1801)=10.2∘

  4. Evaluate

    The sphere leans toward the sheet. Use the insulating-sheet field σ/(2ε₀), not the conductor-surface value σ/ε₀. This is manual problem 22.31, despite the handout numbering 22.33.

θ = 10.2° toward the negative sheet.

Homework 4 · 22.37Flux through a slanted boxSupporting · Gauss & conductors
Original question screenshot

Cropped to question 22.37, with its diagrams and any continuation included. Click an image to enlarge.

Two opposite faces of a box each measure 5.00 cm by 6.00 cm and are inclined 30.0° to a horizontal field. E₁ = 2.50 × 10⁴ N/C points out through one face; E₂ = 7.00 × 10⁴ N/C points in through the other. No field crosses the remaining faces. Find (a) the net enclosed charge and (b) what can be concluded about external charges.

Original problem set ↗Existing homework practice ↗Link to question
Show worked solution

Tesselate explanation

  1. Identify

    Apply Gauss’s law to the entire closed box. The other faces contribute zero by the stated assumption.

  2. Set up

    Each face has A=0.00300 m2A=0.00300\ \mathrm{m^2}A=0.00300 m2. The acute angle between field and face normal is 60∘60^\circ60∘. Φnet=E1Acos⁡60∘−E2Acos⁡60∘,Qenc=ε0Φnet\Phi_{net}=E_1A\cos60^\circ-E_2A\cos60^\circ,\quad Q_{enc}=\varepsilon_0\Phi_{net}Φnet​=E1​Acos60∘−E2​Acos60∘,Qenc​=ε0​Φnet​

  3. Execute

    Φ1=+37.5,Φ2=−105,Φnet=−67.5 N m2/C\Phi_1=+37.5,\quad\Phi_2=-105,\quad\Phi_{net}=-67.5\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C}Φ1​=+37.5,Φ2​=−105,Φnet​=−67.5 Nm2/C (a) Qenc=(8.854×10−12)(−67.5)=−5.98×10−10 C(a)\ Q_{enc}=(8.854\times10^{-12})(-67.5)=-5.98\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm C(a) Qenc​=(8.854×10−12)(−67.5)=−5.98×10−10 C

  4. Evaluate

    (b) The inward net flux proves a negative net enclosed charge. Flux alone cannot determine whether external charges also contribute to the local field: their total closed-surface flux is zero. Do not infer the location of every source from the two field magnitudes; positive and negative charges could both be inside.

Qenc = −5.98 × 10⁻¹⁰ C. External contributions cannot be resolved from net flux alone.

Original question screenshot

Cropped to question 23.1, with its diagrams and any continuation included. Click an image to enlarge.

Fixed q₁ = +2.40 µC at the origin; q₂ = −4.30 µC moves from (0.150, 0) m to (0.250, 0.250) m. Find work done by the electric force.

Original problem set ↗Existing homework practice ↗Link to question
Show worked solution

Tesselate explanation

  1. Identify

    Electric work equals initial minus final potential energy.

  2. Set up

    ri=0.150, rf=0.2502+0.2502; W=kq1q2(1/ri−1/rf)r_i=0.150,\ r_f=\sqrt{0.250^2+0.250^2};\ W=kq_1q_2(1/r_i-1/r_f)ri​=0.150, rf​=0.2502+0.2502​; W=kq1​q2​(1/ri​−1/rf​).

  3. Execute

    rf=0.3536 m; W=(8.988×109)(2.40×10−6)(−4.30×10−6)(6.667−2.828)=−0.356 Jr_f=0.3536\ \mathrm m;\ W=(8.988\times10^9)(2.40\times10^{-6})(-4.30\times10^{-6})(6.667-2.828)=-0.356\ \mathrm Jrf​=0.3536 m; W=(8.988×109)(2.40×10−6)(−4.30×10−6)(6.667−2.828)=−0.356 J.

  4. Evaluate

    Moving unlike charges apart raises potential energy; electric work is negative.

−0.356 J.

Show worked solution

    12mv2+kq1q2/r=12mvi2+kq1q2/ri=Etot\tfrac12mv^2+kq_1q_2/r=\tfrac12mv_i^2+kq_1q_2/r_i=E_{tot}21​mv2+kq1​q2​/r=21​mvi2​+kq1​q2​/ri​=Etot​.

At r=0.400r=0.400r=0.400, K=0.1177 JK=0.1177\ \mathrm JK=0.1177 J, so v=12.5 m/sv=12.5\ \mathrm{m/s}v=12.5 m/s. Original problem set ↗Existing homework practice ↗Link to question
Show worked solution

Tesselate explanation

  1. Identify

  1. Integrate enclosed charge

    Use a dummy radius s; density is not constant across the Gaussian volume. Qenc=∫0rαs2(2πsℓ)ds=παℓr42Q_{\rm enc}=\int_0^r\alpha s^2(2\pi s\ell)ds=\frac{\pi\alpha\ell r^4}{2}Qenc​=∫0r​αs2(2πsℓ)ds=2παℓr4​

  2. Apply Gauss’s law

At the corners of a rectangle of height a = 0.200 m and width b = 0.400 m are +q (upper left), −2q (upper right), +2q (lower left) and +3q (lower right), with q = 6.00 μC. Find the quasistatic assembly energy from infinity.

Original tutorial ↗Full tutorial context ↗Link to question
Show worked solution

    There are two vertical pairs, two horizontal pairs and two diagonal pairs; count each once. Each diagonal has length D = √(a²+b²). U=kq2[2−6a+−2+6b+3−4a2+b2]U=kq^2\left[\frac{2-6}{a}+\frac{-2+6}{b}+\frac{3-4}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\right]U=kq2[a2−6​+b−2+6​+a2+b2​3−4​]

  2. Evaluate the sum

U=(8.988×109)(6.00×10−6)2[−40.200+40.400−10.447214]=−3.959 JU=(8.988\times10^9)(6.00\times10^{-6})^2\left[-\frac4{0.200}+\frac4{0.400}-\frac1{0.447214}\right]=-3.959\ \mathrm JU=(8.988×109)(6.00×10−6)2[−0.2004​+0.4004​−0.4472141​]=−3.959 J

The field graph jumps at charged surfaces, is zero within metal, and decays as 1/r21/r^21/r2 in the two empty regions. Its exterior magnitude is 2kQ/r22kQ/r^22kQ/r2. The central point itself is singular. Field lines from +Q end on the inner surface; exterior lines enter the outer surface.

Two plates of area A and gap d contain dielectric whose relative permittivity increases linearly from 1 to κ along the gap. Find C and the κ → 1 limit.

Link to question
Show worked solution

Tesselate explanation · textbook 15e numbering

  1. Identify series layers

    Let κ(x)=1+(κ−1)x/d\kappa(x)=1+(\kappa-1)x/dκ(x)=1+(κ−1)x/d. Thin layers stack along the field, so add reciprocal capacitances: 1/C=∫0ddx/[ε0Aκ(x)]1/C=\int_0^d dx/[\varepsilon_0A\kappa(x)]1/C=∫0d​dx/[ε0​Aκ(x)].

  2. Integrate and check

    C=ε0Adκ−1ln⁡κ.C=\frac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}\frac{\kappa-1}{\ln\kappa}.C=dε0​A​lnκκ−1​. Since lim⁡κ→1(κ−1)/ln⁡κ=1\lim_{\kappa\to1}(\kappa-1)/\ln\kappa=1limκ→1​(κ−1)/lnκ=1, the air-capacitor limit is correct. This is a series-slice calculation; tilted-plate strips use parallel addition instead.

C = (ε₀A/d)(κ − 1)/ln κ.

    C(x)=ε0LD[L+(κ−1)x],C′=ε0LD(κ−1).C(x)=\frac{\varepsilon_0L}{D}[L+(\kappa-1)x],\qquad C'=\frac{\varepsilon_0L}{D}(\kappa-1).C(x)=Dε0​L​[L+(κ−1)x],C′=Dε0​L​(κ−1).

  2. Compare constraints and include the battery

    At fixed VVV, dU=+12V2C′ dxdU=+\tfrac12V^2C'\,dxdU=+21​V2C′dx. At fixed QQQ, dU=−Q2C′ dx/(2C2)=−12V2C′ dxdU=-Q^2C'\,dx/(2C^2)=-\tfrac12V^2C'\,dxdU=−Q2C′dx/(2C2)=−21​V2C′dx, where V is the instantaneous voltage and initially Q=C(x)VQ=C(x)VQ=C(x)V. For the battery-connected system, dWbattery=V dQ=V2C′ dxdW_{\rm battery}=V\,dQ=V^2C'\,dxdWbattery​=VdQ=V2C′dx. Subtract the capacitor’s energy increase: F dx=dWbattery−dU=12V2C′ dxF\,dx=dW_{\rm battery}-dU=\tfrac12V^2C'\,dxFdx=dWbattery​−dU=21​V2C′dx.

F = ε₀L(κ − 1)V²/(2D), pulling the slab farther into the capacitor.

HIGH-PRIORITY PREPARATION / REPORTED BOARD HINT

A tilted capacitor: solve for the angle

You reported that the instructor drew a capacitor with its top plate at an angle and discussed solving for that angle. Treat the first model below as high-priority preparation. The exact givens and any dielectric or mechanical constraints are still unknown; the written October 28 announcement does not specify tilt.

1. One plate tilted relative to the other

L is the projected overlap length, w is the width into the page, and d₀ is the near-edge gap. The strip approximation assumes a small angle, locally parallel fields and negligible fringing.

d(x)=d0+xtan⁡θ.d(x)=d_0+x\tan\theta.d(x)=d0​+xtanθ. dC=κε0w dxd(x).dC=\frac{\kappa\varepsilon_0w\,dx}{d(x)}.dC=d(x)κε0​wdx​. C(θ)≈κε0wtan⁡θln⁡(1+Ltan⁡θd0).C(\theta)\approx\frac{\kappa\varepsilon_0w}{\tan\theta}\ln\left(1+\frac{L\tan\theta}{d_0}\right).C(θ)≈tanθκε0​w​ln(1+d0​Ltanθ​).

The strips share a voltage, so they are in parallel. Given Q and V, use C = Q/V first. Keep the near-edge gap fixed when varying θ in this model.

Worked example and limiting check

For d₀ = 1.00 mm, L = 100 mm, w = 50 mm and κ = 1, the parallel value is 44.2709 pF. A measured capacitance of approximately 25.6156 pF corresponds to θ ≈ 1.00°. Substitute trial angles or use bisection: C decreases monotonically as θ increases. The expression returns ε₀κwL/d₀ as θ approaches zero.

Calculator searches 0–10°. This is a numerical range, not a guarantee of model accuracy; a physical result also needs gaps small compared with plate dimensions.

2. Parallel plates tilted in a liquid dielectric

Start from the fuel-gauge question, HW7 24.68 / textbook 24.66. When each area is filled across the entire gap, air and liquid areas are parallel:

C=ε0d[A+(κ−1)Aliquid(θ)],Aliquid=Cd/ε0−Aκ−1.C=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{d}[A+(\kappa-1)A_{\rm liquid}(\theta)],\quad A_{\rm liquid}=\frac{Cd/\varepsilon_0-A}{\kappa-1}. C=dε0​​[A+(κ−1)Aliquid​(θ)],Aliquid​=κ−1Cd/ε0​−A​.

Use the pictured pivot, liquid level and plate dimensions to turn that area into θ. If an individual field path crosses both air and liquid, first combine those layers in series, then integrate parallel strips:

C≈∫ε0w dxdair(x,θ)+dliquid(x,θ)/κ.C\approx\int\frac{\varepsilon_0w\,dx}{d_{\rm air}(x,\theta)+d_{\rm liquid}(x,\theta)/\kappa}.C≈∫dair​(x,θ)+dliquid​(x,θ)/κε0​wdx​.

No unique numerical angle follows without the liquid level and pivot geometry. Rotating a uniformly filled parallel-plate capacitor as a whole, without changing its gap or filling, does not change its ideal capacitance.

3. A charged ball hangs at an angle between plates

Reverse HW6 23.59. For vertical plates and a horizontal field:

Tsin⁡θ=∣q∣E,Tcos⁡θ=mg,θ=tan⁡−1 ⁣(∣q∣ ∣ΔV∣mgd).T\sin\theta=|q|E,\quad T\cos\theta=mg,\quad \theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{|q|\,|\Delta V|}{mgd}\right).Tsinθ=∣q∣E,Tcosθ=mg,θ=tan−1(mgd∣q∣∣ΔV∣​).

Using m = 1.50 g, |q| = 8.90 µC, d = 5.00 cm and ΔV ≈ 47.7 V gives θ ≈ 30.0°. A mechanically rotating plate instead requires a torque balance and its support geometry.
